summary: This RFC proposes a Telnet option for sending a banner from the server to the user's Telnet, to be shown on the screen independently of the application. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 933 proposes a Telnet option for sending a screen banner separately from normal application output. After both sides agree, the user's Telnet displays and maintains the banner.

questions: what is the output marking telnet option
how to display a banner in telnet
what is the telnet output marking option
how do telnet security banners work
subtitle: A Telnet option for keeping a server-supplied banner visible on the user's screen.

tldr.problem: Some systems need a security banner on the user's display, but sending it repeatedly as ordinary application output is inefficient.
tldr.mechanism: Telnet peers negotiate OUTMRK, then the server sends banner text and a placement flag for the user's Telnet to display independently.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes a Telnet option that lets the user-side software maintain the marking until the server ends it or the option is refused.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 933's status as Proposed Standard. The RFC presents OUTMRK as a proposed Telnet option and requests discussion and suggestions.

sections.title: Why Send a Separate Screen Banner
sections.content:
The RFC describes systems that associate a security level with a Telnet connection and need to show a security banner on the display. Sending the banner in every screen of application data makes the server responsible for the display's page size and repeats information.

With OUTMRK, the server sends the marking once with instructions, and the user's Telnet keeps it displayed. A control flag allows the marking to be placed at the top, bottom, left, right, or at the user's discretion.
sections.plainLanguage: The option lets a server provide a banner without repeating it in every screen of application output. The user's Telnet handles where the banner appears.

sections.title: Agreeing to Use OUTMRK
sections.content:
Either side can initiate the option, though the server normally requests output marking. The peers use Telnet's WILL, DO, WON'T, and DON'T commands to agree before the server sends the marking data in a subnegotiation.

The user-side Telnet responds with ACK if the data is acceptable or NAK if it objects. After acceptance, it maps application output into the remaining screen area; the server can end marking by sending WON'T OUTMRK.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server first agree that they can exchange output markings. The client then accepts or rejects the banner data.

sections.title: Banner Text and Placement
sections.content:
The marking data is ASCII text, and the control flag indicates the intended placement: default, top, bottom, left, or right. The RFC says the precise meaning of left and right placement is not defined.

Carriage Return and Line Feed separate lines in a multiline banner. Multiple banners can be sent in one subnegotiation, separated by the ASCII Group Separator character.
sections.plainLanguage: The banner contains text and a placement instruction. Line breaks separate banner lines, and a separator can divide multiple markings.
